original_value: A fascinating challenge in the field of human–robot interaction is the possibility to endow robots with emotional intelligence in order to make the interaction more intuitive, genuine, and natural. To achieve this, a critical point is the capability of the robot to infer and interpret human emotions. Emotion recognition has been widely explored in the broader fields of human–machine interaction and affective computing. Here, we report recent advances in emotion recognition, with particular regard to the human–robot interaction context. Our aim is to review the state of the art of currently adopted emotional models, interaction modalities, and classification strategies and offer our point of view on future developments and critical issues. We focus on facial expressions, body poses and kinematics, voice, brain activity, and peripheral physiological responses, also providing a list of available datasets containing data from these modalities.

result.paraphrase: A key challenge in human–robot interaction is giving robots emotional intelligence so interactions feel more intuitive, authentic, and natural. Achieving this depends on the robot’s ability to infer and interpret human emotions. Emotion recognition has been extensively studied in human–machine interaction and affective computing. In this work, we summarize recent progress in emotion recognition, especially within the human–robot interaction setting. We aim to review the current state of the art in emotional models, interaction modalities, and classification methods, and to share our perspective on future directions and open issues. We concentrate on facial expressions, body posture and kinematics, voice, brain activity, and peripheral physiological responses, and we also provide a list of available datasets covering these modalities.
